description: #Astroflare is a student team driven by curiosity, creativity and a passion for turning ideas into working prototypes. Our interests include engineering, coding, robotics and design. Join us to build practical solutions, learn together and contribute from concept to presentation. We're looking for enthusiastic teammates with skills in programming, electronics, CAD, research or storytelling. Commitment, teamwork and a willingness to learn matter just as much as experience.
summary: Astro Flare is a research planning website that helps students and combustion researchers identify relevant NASA experiments and decide what to investigate next. Built for Flame in Freefall, it transforms curated records from NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics repository BASS-II, Saffire I, and Saffire II into an interactive evidence explorer. Users can launch a hypothetical lunar habitat demonstration, filter experiments by material and test conditions, compare investigations, and retrieve cited answers. Explained rankings show why studies are relevant, while a research takeaway connects measured findings, evidence gaps, and proposed follow-up work. Users can copy a research brief containing the original NASA citations. Scientific context remains central. A fabric’s measured flame-spread rate is not reused as a silicone result, and microgravity measurements are not presented as lunar predictions. Astro Flare makes NASA’s combustion research easier to inspect and use responsibly. It helps users develop proposals grounded in real measurements while making unanswered questions visible the starting point for the next experiment.
details:
AstroFlare is a research planning website developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, Flame in Freefall. It addresses one focused problem: helping students and combustion researchers determine which NASA experiments are relevant to their scenario, what those experiments actually demonstrate, and what still needs investigation. Its central question is: “Which evidence can inform this scenario, and what should we test next?”

The project uses NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics repository, including BASS-II (PSI-25), Saffire I (PSI-98), and Saffire II (PSI-99). The current collection contains eight selected experimental rows across these three investigations. Records preserve material information, gravity regime, oxygen concentration, airflow, measured outcomes, units, and original NASA citations. Source-file versions, row identifiers, and file hashes support traceability. Missing values remain explicitly labelled rather than being estimated.

Users can launch a public lunar habitat demonstration with one click or explore their own research question. Reproducible matching rules rank investigations by research relevance and explain their placement. Material, experimental-gravity, and airflow filters narrow the evidence, while a separate scenario-gravity control highlights limits in applying those results. Users can compare two investigations side by side, ask supported evidence questions, inspect original sources, and copy a cited research brief. The “What should we test next?” panel connects three elements: what NASA measured, what remains unknown for the selected scenario, and a proposed follow-up investigation.

Astro Flare’s creative contribution is making scientific uncertainty interactive and useful. For example, Saffire II run 2-5 reports a flame-spread rate of 2.1 mm/s for SIBAL cotton–fibre glass material in microgravity. Selecting silicone changes the supporting evidence to run 2-1, whose table describes burn time as “Insignificant” and provides no spread rate. The application preserves that distinction and updates the research takeaway. An original interactive experiment schematic also lets users explore these material-specific findings; it is clearly labelled as a schematic rather than experimental imagery.

The interface uses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with SVG for schematic artwork and data visualisation. Node.js serves the application and API routes, while Python supports the build process and the separate mission-screening engine. Curated evidence is stored in JSON, alongside original CSV source files. The deployment uses Docker on Render. Automated checks use Node’s test runner, jsdom, and Python’s unittest framework. The project is software based and requires no dedicated sensors or laboratory hardware. Core evidence lookup and ranking are deterministic; optional AI explanations are separate from the cited results and are labelled unreviewed.

The intended beneficiaries are students, educators, and university combustion laboratories. A student preparing a material-flammability proposal can identify a relevant measurement, inspect its conditions, and explain why additional investigation is necessary. A laboratory can use the comparison workflow to identify differences between published experiments and its proposed conditions. The intended impact is better-supported research planning; improvements in research efficiency still require evaluation with users.

Scientific accuracy, accessibility, and reliability shaped the design. Research relevance remains separate from fire-risk scoring. Microgravity measurements are never treated as direct lunar-gravity predictions, and proposed experiments remain distinct from completed research. Keyboard access, mobile layouts, reduced-motion preferences, missing-data messages, and recovery from service failures support usability. Expanding the verified collection could extend this approach to more materials and conditions, helping researchers turn NASA’s existing evidence into clearer questions for the next experiment.
